Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

I feel like I don't know myself anymore
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette: The ambush had unfolded in a narrow, wind-scoured valley during his third year overseas, a moment that still fractures Arthur Vance’s breathing thirty-five years later. He had been moving through the jagged ravine when the sudden, deafening snap of automatic fire and the heavy thud of boots against shale broke their formation. When the dust settled, Arthur was the only one left standing among his squad mates. In the years since, the memory of that valley refused to settle into a coherent narrative. He knew exactly what had transpired, yet he would sit at his kitchen table and stare at his coffee cup, unable to find the words to describe it to his partner or to himself. The silence in his head was always followed by a rush of terror identical to the one he felt when the rifles opened up. That terror quickly curdled into a heavy, unshakable conviction that he had no right to draw his next breath while others lay dead in the dirt. He felt like a ghost in his own life, certain that the foundation of who he was had been burned away in that valley, leaving behind a man who could not recognize his own reflection. The world, he had come to believe, was an inherently dangerous place where safety was an illusion and death could strike without warning. His survival guilt and the conviction that the world remained a hostile environment ensured that the memory would never fade; instead, every quiet moment summoned the same terror he felt at the time, locking the past into the present. Because Arthur’s internal narrative framed his identity as permanently fractured and his surroundings as fundamentally unsafe, his daily life began to shrink. He stopped wearing dark, rugged field jackets or heavy wool trousers, finding the texture and color of similar clothes unbearable against his skin. He avoided going near places with steep drop-offs or confined, echoing spaces, telling himself it was merely a preference for open, flat terrain. The terror that surged in his chest whenever the valley’s geography crossed his mind convinced him that he needed to shield himself from any resemblance to the past, so he systematically avoided thinking about the event altogether. Yet, by refusing to process the memory, he only reinforced the conviction that he was fundamentally broken. Every time he turned away from a familiar texture or clamped down on a thought, the world grew marginally more dangerous in his estimation, and the guilt over surviving felt heavier than before. He was certain that the only way to stay safe was to keep moving, to keep his head down, and to never look back, even though the strategy was slowly starving him of his own peace. Arthur worked as a warehouse worker, a job that initially offered the predictable rhythm he craved, but the high ceilings and concrete aisles of the distribution center eventually became a new landscape of threat. When he walked past the loading bays on his break, the smell of heated metal and the low hum of forklifts aligned with the terrain of the ambush site, forcing him to step back and cross the street rather than face the space. His avoidance of the location had become a rigid rule, one that dictated his routes and his breathing. The guilt that accompanied the memory would not let him rest, and the terror on recall would directly feed back into his negative appraisals, convincing him once more that he was fundamentally broken and that the world was an unforgiving place. He found himself retreating into the same mental habits that had kept him alive in the valley, even as they hollowed out the life he had built. At sixty, the exhaustion of maintaining the distance finally outweighed the fear of facing the past. Arthur sat in the therapist’s office, his hands resting on his knees, wondering if it was possible to reclaim the man he used to be. He was most afraid that the terror would return with a strength he could no longer outrun, but he hoped that talking about the valley might finally give him the words he had been searching for. He wanted to stop flinching at the sound of heavy doors slamming, wanted to wear a simple jacket without waiting for his stomach to turn, and wanted to believe that he could walk through a parking lot without calculating every exit. The memory and the dread were still there, but for the first time in decades, Arthur was willing to let them sit in the room with him.
